name: Tussore
lede: Tussore is a pale yellowish pink from the Maerz and Paul color dictionary, named for tussore silk, the wild, undyed Indian and Chinese silk it resembles.

sections.title: The color of raw silk
sections.body:
Maerz and Paul record Tussore at #E3C9B2, first dated 1887, on plate 10 A4 of their 1930 dictionary [1]. The name comes from tussore, also spelled tusser or tussah, a coarse wild silk woven in India and China [1]. It was traditionally left undyed, in its own pale tan [1]. The books consulted do not spell out this link explicitly, so it is given here as the plain sense of the word rather than a sourced etymology [1].

Its nearest named neighbor in our library is [[sandust]], very slightly cooler [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our archive finds this hue, as photographed, in 1,006 of 23,781 paintings (4.23 percent), more common than 86 percent of the named colors we track [2]. It peaks in the 1200s, in 7 of 142 paintings, at 1.6 times the expected rate for the 142 paintings we have from that century [2]. Inside a painting it most often plays a light, in 46 percent of its 678 occurrences [2].

[[painter:xugu|Xugu]] is its most devoted painter here, carrying it in 9 of 16 of his works, 7.5 times his home museums' baseline [2]. It is most over-represented in paintings from India, at 2.4 times the expected rate, fitting for a name drawn from Indian silk [2]. It shares canvases more than chance with [[light-brownish-drab]] and [[japan-rose]] [2].
